title_options: Is Scrolling Before Bed Bad? What the Evidence Actually Shows
Is Scrolling Before Bed Bad? Light, Lost Time, and the Wired Feeling
Is Scrolling Before Bed Bad for Sleep? An Honest Answer (It's Probably Not the Blue Light)
search_intent: Informational/explainer. The searcher wants a direct yes/no answer on whether bedtime scrolling hurts sleep, plus a reason they can trust. Underneath that: they want to know whether blue light and night mode matter, and why some nights they fall asleep fine while other nights they lie awake wired.
serp_summary: Sleep-product brands (sleep.com/Mattress Firm, Emma, Turmerry, a mattress retailer), news write-ups of single studies (CBS Boston, ConsumerAffairs, Get Surrey) and one app blog hold the top spots. Most are listicles that answer "yes, it's bad" right away, treat blue light as settled, recommend night mode or blue-light glasses, overstate causation from correlational or sponsor data, apply teen findings to adults, and give all-or-nothing advice like phone bans. None separates light, bedtime displacement and arousal, and none gives the reader a way to check their own experience.
gaps: Honest answer up front: not automatically bad; the 2024 expert panel reached no consensus on screen light, or on screens in adults at all
Separate the three mechanisms (light, displacement, arousal), each with its own evidence strength
Nuance on light: a modest effect for most, but individual sensitivity varies more than 50-fold (Phillips 2019)
Night mode verdict backed by the BYU 2021 study (no difference)
Sleep pressure explains why some nights are fine and others aren't
A drowsy-or-wired self-test for the moment you put the phone down
Teen vs adult evidence kept distinct; correlation vs causation stated plainly
A short slow-exhale note for the wired case, with honest limits on the evidence

outline.h2: Is scrolling before bed bad? The short answer
points: 40-60 word quotable answer: not automatically; for most adults light is probably a smaller factor than headlines suggest; how late you stay up and how wound up you are when you stop matter more
16-expert panel: consensus for kids and teens, no consensus on light for anyone or on adults (S1)
Hjetland 2025: time in bed with screens predicted insomnia odds; social media was no worse than other screen activities (S2)
Frame as state over minutes: how you feel when you stop

outline.h2: Three ways a bedtime scroll can affect sleep
points: Light, displacement and arousal are different mechanisms with different evidence
Summary table: mechanism | what the evidence shows | strength for adults | what helps
Most articles blend these together; separating them tells you which one applies to you

outline.h2: Does blue light from your phone really suppress melatonin?
points: Chang 2015: 55% melatonin suppression and onset 1.5+ h later, but from 4 h of reading for 5 nights in a dim lab (S3)
Höhn 2024: 90 min of phone reading lowered melatonin, but whole-night sleep was largely unaffected; males only (S5)
Zeitzer: phones give about 25-50 lux vs 10,000+ for sunlight; adult eyes let in less light (S9, expert opinion)
Phillips 2019: group ED50 about 25 lux, individual range 6-350 lux, so the effect is small for most and possibly bigger for some (S4)

outline.h2: Does night mode or Night Shift help you sleep?
points: BYU 2021, 167 adults aged 18-24: no difference between Night Shift on, Night Shift off, and no phone (S7, S8)
Salzburg: filters only partly soften the effect (S6)
Verdict: fine to leave on, but don't count on it; skip blue-light glasses (no evidence in this brief)

outline.h2: The bigger factor: 'one more' and a later bedtime
points: About 24 fewer minutes of sleep per extra hour of screen use in bed (S2)
Bedtime procrastination as the mechanism (S10, adolescent and cross-sectional caveat)
Cross-sectional data: poor sleepers may also scroll more

outline.h2: Why some content leaves you wired
points: Zeitzer: emotionally activating content probably matters more than light; calming content works for some people (S9)
BYU researchers point to psychological stimulation separate from light (S8)
Singapore General Hospital: duration and emotional stimulation matter more (S12)
Plausible and expert-backed, but the panel found no consensus for adults (S1)

outline.h2: Why you fall asleep fine some nights and lie awake on others
points: Sleep pressure: Jensen's line that when you're very tired you fall asleep regardless (S7)
Your own sensitivity varies (S4), and so does what you scrolled
Notice how you feel at the moment you put the phone down
Drowsy: the scroll is probably harmless, or mainly costing you time; look at the bedtime cutoff
Wired (busy mind, tight jaw, heart a little quick): arousal is the likely issue
Optional cutoff of about an hour is expert advice, not tested in these studies (S9, S5)

outline.h2: If you're wired: a slow-exhale breath to come down
points: Calm 4-6 breath for 60 seconds; link the /tools/ calm 4-6 tool and the night doomscrolling post for the full routine
Laborde 2019: 15 min per night for 30 days improved self-reported sleep and vagal activity vs social media (S11); a 60-second version is less tested
Tsai 2020: HRV rose but measured sleep didn't change robustly (S13), so be honest it calms you in the moment
Safety note; at most one felt-experience DeRot mention (pre-launch)

key_facts.fact: A 16-expert panel found no consensus on whether screen light impairs sleep, or whether screen time, light or content affects adults; consensus was reached only for children and adolescents.
Each extra hour of screen use after going to bed was linked to 59% higher odds of insomnia symptoms and 24 fewer minutes of sleep in 45,202 students aged 18-28.
In that study, social media was no worse than other screen activities; overall time in bed mattered more.
Reading on a light-emitting eReader for 4 hours over 5 evenings suppressed melatonin by 55% and delayed its onset by more than 1.5 hours.
In the eReader study, falling asleep took about 10 minutes longer (25.7 vs 15.8 min).
Half-maximal melatonin suppression occurred at about 24.6 lux on average, with individual sensitivity ranging from 6 to 350 lux, a more than 50-fold difference.
90 minutes of phone reading lowered melatonin, but whole-night sleep was largely unaffected in males aged 14-25.
Blue-light filters only partially mitigate the effects of evening smartphone light.
In 167 adults aged 18-24, sleep did not differ between Night Shift on, Night Shift off, or no phone in the hour before bed.
Phone screens at night give roughly 25-50 lux, compared with 10,000-100,000 lux in sunlight (Zeitzer, Stanford).
15 minutes of slow breathing at about 6 breaths per minute each evening for 30 days improved self-reported sleep quality compared with 15 minutes of social media.
30 minutes of presleep slow breathing raised HRV but had no robust effect on polysomnographic sleep in a 20-person pilot.

safety_notes: Never claim breathing or changing phone habits treats insomnia; if poor sleep lasts most nights for weeks or affects your days, talk to a doctor or sleep specialist.
State that Hjetland 2025 is cross-sectional: poor sleepers may scroll more, not only the other way round.
Breathing: keep it gentle and stop if dizzy or lightheaded; avoid breath holds and fast breathing if pregnant, if you have heart or lung conditions, or if you have a history of fainting or panic.
If the wired feeling is recurring anxiety or distress, point readers to a professional; if they may be in crisis, point to local emergency services or 988 in the US.
Never write 'blue light doesn't matter'; sensitivity varies widely between people.
Present tips as options, not rules: no guilt about minutes and no phone bans. DeRot is pre-launch.

# Research notes: "Is scrolling before bed bad?"

## SERP ANALYSIS

**Who ranks:** The top results are mostly sleep-product brands (sleep.com, which is owned by Mattress Firm; Emma Sleep; Turmerry; a mattress retailer's blog), news write-ups of single studies (CBS Boston, ConsumerAffairs, Get Surrey, To Vima), and one app blog (habitdoom.com, "2026 Research"). Few clinical or university pages show up for the exact query. For related queries, CU Boulder, Stanford Lifestyle Medicine, Frontiers and the BYU news coverage show up.

**Format:** Mostly listicle-style explainers with a "why it's bad" section, a "how to stop" section, and tips. They answer "yes, it's bad" in the first lines.

**What they do well:**
- They name doomscrolling and emotional content as a factor, not only light.
- They give practical tips (set a cutoff, charge the phone elsewhere, Do Not Disturb).

**What they miss or get wrong:**
- **Causation is overstated.** Sleep.com's headline frames the evidence as proof, but most of what it cites is correlational, and some of it is the sponsor's own SleepScore research with no published methods.
- **Blue light is stated as settled.** Several pages say screens "trick your brain into thinking it's daytime" and recommend blue-light glasses with no evidence. None mention that the [16-expert Sleep Health panel](https://www.colorado.edu/today/2024/05/28/light-or-content-what-we-know-about-screens-and-sleep-disruption) could not reach consensus on whether screen light impairs anyone's sleep, or on whether screen time, light or content affects adults.
- **Night mode is still recommended** without mentioning the [BYU Night Shift study](https://sleepreviewmag.com/sleep-treatments/therapy-devices/emerging-technology/apples-night-shift-help-sleep/), which found no difference.
- **The three mechanisms are blended together.** Nobody separates light, bedtime displacement, and arousal, or says which one probably matters for a given person.
- **No self-check.** No page helps a reader work out whether their own scrolling is a problem. The reader's actual experience (some nights fine, some nights wired) goes unexplained.
- **The advice is all-or-nothing:** phones out of the bedroom, or a 60 to 90 minute screen ban. Nothing addresses the moment you put the phone down feeling wired.
- **Teen data is applied to adults.** The "90% of studies" figure on sleep.com comes from a review of children and adolescents.

## GAPS AND ANGLE

1. **Honest answer up front:** "Not automatically. For most adults the light is probably a smaller factor than the headlines suggest. What matters more is how long you stay up and how wound up you are when you stop." Back this with the Sleep Health panel (no consensus on light, or on adults at all) and Hjetland 2025 (time in bed predicted insomnia odds; social media was no worse than other screen activities).
2. **Separate the three mechanisms, each with its own evidence:**
   - **Light.** The effect is real in the lab. Chang 2015 found 55% melatonin suppression and a 1.5-hour delay in melatonin onset, but that was 4 hours of reading a night for 5 nights in a dim lab. Höhn 2024 found melatonin was lower after 90 minutes of phone reading, but whole-night sleep was largely unaffected.
   - **Nuance on light:** [Phillips 2019](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6575863) found a more than 50-fold difference in light sensitivity between individuals, with a group ED50 (the light level that suppresses melatonin by half) of about 25 lux. That is roughly the 25 to 50 lux Stanford's Zeitzer estimates for a phone at night. So "light is a small factor" should be written as "small for most, possibly bigger for some." This is honest nuance competitors miss.
   - **Displacement.** About 24 fewer minutes of sleep per extra hour of screen use in bed (Hjetland 2025). Bedtime procrastination, the "one more" loop, fits here.
   - **Arousal.** Zeitzer (Stanford) points to emotionally activating content. The panel reached consensus that content impairs sleep in youth, but not for adults, so present arousal as plausible and supported by experts rather than proven for adults.
3. **Night mode verdict:** BYU 2021 (167 adults aged 18 to 24) found no difference between Night Shift on, Night Shift off, and no phone. The Höhn studies found blue-light filters only partly soften the light effect. Takeaway: night mode is fine to keep on, but don't count on it.
4. **Sleep pressure explains "some nights fine, some nights wired."** Jensen: when you're very tired, "you fall asleep no matter what you did just before bed." This directly explains the reader's experience.
5. **The drowsy-or-wired test:** Notice how you feel when you put the phone down. Drowsy suggests the scroll is mostly harmless or just eating time. Wired (busy mind, tight jaw, heart a little quick) suggests arousal. Then add a short slow-exhale note: Laborde 2019 is the closest relevant evidence, though it was 15 minutes a night for 30 days, not 60 seconds. Link the calm 4-6 breathing tool and the existing night doomscrolling post for the routine. Keep any DeRot mention to the felt experience (the wired feeling fading); it is pre-launch.
6. **Possible table:** mechanism | what the evidence shows | how strong it is for adults | what helps.

## QUESTIONS (People Also Ask style)

- Is it bad to scroll on your phone before bed?
- Why can't I sleep after scrolling on my phone, even with night mode on?
- Does night mode or Night Shift actually help you sleep?
- Is blue light from phones really that bad for sleep?
- How long before bed should I stop using my phone? (Sources give 30 to 60 minutes or about an hour. That is expert advice and was not directly tested in these studies.)
- Is social media worse than watching TV or reading on my phone before bed?
- Why do I sometimes fall asleep fine after scrolling and other nights lie awake?
- Do blue-light glasses help?
- Is it okay to watch calming videos to fall asleep? (Zeitzer notes some people use calming content like nature videos.)
- What should I do if I feel wired after scrolling in bed?

## SOURCES

https://www.colorado.edu/today/2024/05/28/light-or-content-what-we-know-about-screens-and-sleep-disruption | The light or the content? What we know about screens and sleep disruption | University of Colorado Boulder (reporting a Sleep Health / National Sleep Foundation consensus paper) | 2024 | 16 sleep experts screened over 2,200 articles, including 35 experimental studies and 5 systematic reviews. Consensus reached that screen use and pre-sleep screen content impair sleep in children and adolescents, and that behavioral strategies may help. No consensus on whether screen light impairs sleep for anyone, or whether screen time, light or content affects adults. Hartstein quote: "But the current data are not strong enough for us to say conclusively that it has a direct effect." Also: "This is not to say that the panel concluded light from screens does not impact sleep." Adults may be less affected by content (mature brains, less FOMO). Working US adults sleeping under 7 hours rose from 30.9% (2010) to 35.6% (2018).

https://www.frontiersin.org/news/2025/03/31/hours-screen-use-after-bed-increases-insomnia-risk-frontiers-psychiatry | Hours of screen use after bed increases insomnia risk | Frontiers (news release for Hjetland et al., Frontiers in Psychiatry, DOI 10.3389/fpsyt.2025.1548273) | 2025 | 45,202 Norwegian full-time students aged 18 to 28 (2022 Students' Health and Wellbeing survey). Each extra hour of screen use after going to bed: 59% higher odds of insomnia symptoms and 24 fewer minutes of sleep. No significant difference between social media and other screen activities. Hjetland: "The type of screen activity does not appear to matter as much as the overall time spent using screens in bed." Cross-sectional, so causality is unclear; no physiological measures; one culture. Note: some outlets reported 63%, so use 59% from the release.

https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25535358/ | Evening use of light-emitting eReaders negatively affects sleep, circadian timing, and next-morning alertness (Chang et al.) | PNAS | 2015 | 12 healthy adults (mean age about 25) read for 4 hours before bed on 5 consecutive evenings, light-emitting eBook vs printed book, in a dim inpatient lab, crossover design. eBook: melatonin suppressed 55% vs none; melatonin onset more than 1.5 hours later (22:31 vs 21:01); sleep latency about 10 minutes longer (25.7 vs 15.8 min); less REM (109 vs 121 min); less alert next morning. eBook light was about 32 lux, peaking around 452 nm. Authors called it a mechanistic study, not a field study. The 4-hour dose is far above typical scrolling.

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6575863 | High sensitivity and interindividual variability in the response of the human circadian system to evening light (Phillips et al.) | PNAS (Monash / Brigham and Women's) | 2019 | 55 healthy adults aged 18 to 30, exposed to 10 to 2,000 lux for 5 hours in the evening. Group ED50 (light level giving 50% melatonin suppression) about 24.6 lux. Individual ED50 ranged from 6 to 350 lux, a more than 50-fold difference. 10, 30 and 50 lux delayed melatonin onset by 22, 77 and 109 minutes. Some people respond to ordinary indoor light almost like daylight; others barely respond. Lab exposure was room light, not phones.

https://academic.oup.com/braincomms/article/6/3/fcae173/7675955 | Effects of evening smartphone use on sleep and declarative memory consolidation in male adolescents and young adults (Höhn et al.) | Brain Communications | 2024 | 33 male adolescents (14 to 17) and 35 male young adults (18 to 25), three polysomnography nights: 90 minutes reading on a phone without a filter, with a blue-light filter, or a printed book; bedtime about 50 minutes later. No effect on subjective sleepiness. Unfiltered phone lowered melatonin in both groups; adolescents recovered by bedtime, adults still had lower melatonin. Whole-night sleep and N3 largely unaffected (adults: less N3 in the first quarter of the night only). Memory consolidation unaffected. Authors: "Nighttime smartphone reading does not appear to interfere with whole-night sleep..." but still advise avoiding phones in the last hour before bed. Males only.

https://www.plus.ac.at/news/impact-of-evening-smartphone-use/?lang=en | Impact of evening smartphone use | University of Salzburg (press release for Höhn, Schmid et al., Clocks & Sleep 2021, DOI 10.3390/clockssleep3010005) | 2021 | Pilot with 14 people over 4 lab nights, 90 minutes reading on a phone with or without a blue-light filter, or a book. Short-wavelength light affected melatonin, evening sleepiness and sleep physiology, and lowered next-morning alertness. Quote: "Blue light filters can only partially mitigate negative effects on sleep." Search snippets described a 33-man expanded paper (melatonin rise blunted in both phone conditions, less slow-wave sleep early in the night with the unfiltered phone; evening positive mood predicted better subjective but not objective sleep). I couldn't open that paper, so the writer should cite only the press-release facts.

https://sleepreviewmag.com/sleep-treatments/therapy-devices/emerging-technology/apples-night-shift-help-sleep/ | Does Apple's Night Shift help sleep? | Sleep Review (reporting BYU / Cincinnati Children's study in Sleep Health) | 2021 | 167 adults aged 18 to 24 who use phones daily, spending at least 8 hours in bed. Groups: phone with Night Shift, phone without Night Shift, or no phone in the hour before bed, 7 nights, wrist accelerometer. Whole sample: no differences in sleep duration, quality, wake after sleep onset or time to fall asleep. Among those averaging about 7 hours of sleep, the no-phone group had slightly better quality. Among those under 6 hours, no difference. Jensen: "Night Shift is not superior to using your phone without Night Shift or even using no phone at all." Also: "when you are super tired you fall asleep no matter what you did just before bed."

https://magazine.byu.edu/article/good-night-night-mode | Night Mode Doesn't Actually Improve Sleep, BYU Researchers Find | BYU Magazine | 2021 | University source for the same study (167 participants, ages 18 to 24). Researchers suggest psychological stimulation from phone use is a sleep-deterring factor separate from light. Good alternative citation for the Night Shift finding.

https://lifestylemedicine.stanford.edu/screen-time-and-sleep-its-different-for-adults | Screen Time and Sleep: It's Different for Adults | Stanford Lifestyle Medicine (Jamie Zeitzer, PhD, Co-Director, Stanford Center for Sleep and Circadian Sciences) | undated, about 2024 | Phone screens at night give about 25 to 50 lux, vs 10,000 to 100,000 lux in sunlight. Adults have smaller pupils and more lens opacity than children, so less light reaches the retina. Argues emotionally activating content (social media, games, streaming) matters more than light, and that responses vary by person (some use calming content like nature videos to fall asleep). Suggests avoiding distressing or exciting content and a rough cutoff of about an hour. This is expert opinion, so attribute it as such, and note it conflicts somewhat with Phillips 2019 on low-lux sensitivity.

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11059092 | The Association Between Bedtime Procrastination, Sleep Quality, and Problematic Smartphone Use in Adolescents: A Mediation Analysis | Eurasian Journal of Medicine (PMC) | 2024 | 245 adolescents in Turkey, averaging 2.3 hours a day of phone use in bed. Bedtime procrastination mediated the link between problematic phone use and poor sleep quality. Cross-sectional, adolescent sample. Use only to support the "one more" displacement mechanism, with a caveat. Avoid its "problematic use" framing.

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6406675/ | Influence of a 30-Day Slow-Paced Breathing Intervention Compared to Social Media Use on Subjective Sleep Quality and Cardiac Vagal Activity (Laborde et al.) | Journal of Clinical Medicine | 2019 | RCT, 64 analyzed (healthy, mean age 22). About 6 breaths per minute (4.5 s in, 5.5 s out) for 15 minutes each evening before sleep for 30 days, vs 15 minutes of social media before sleep. Breathing group: better subjective sleep quality on the PSQI (d = 0.51) and higher overnight vagal activity (HF-HRV, d = 0.68); social media group: no significant change. Limits: self-reported sleep, no polysomnography, young healthy sample, longer practice than a 60-second reset.

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7198497/ | The Effects of Presleep Slow Breathing and Music Listening on Polysomnographic Sleep Measures: a pilot trial | Scientific Reports | 2020 | 20 young adults, randomized crossover: 30 minutes of slow breathing vs music vs control. Both raised HRV immediately, but neither had robust effects on polysomnographic sleep quality. Useful honesty check: slow breathing reliably calms the body in the moment, but evidence that it improves measured sleep is mixed.

Lower-priority sources (SERP context only, don't cite for health claims): https://www.sleep.com/sleep-health/doomscrolling (Mattress Firm-owned; SleepScore poll of 2,526 people: 71% scroll before bed, no methods given) and https://www.sgh.com.sg/news/patient-care/is-your-phone-keeping-you-awake-4-tips-for-sleep-deprived-sporeans (Singapore General Hospital: experts say how long you use the phone near bedtime and how emotionally stimulating the content is matter more in delaying sleep. Could serve as a clinic-level supporting citation.)

## SAFETY

- **No treatment claims.** Don't say breathing or changing phone habits treats insomnia. Persistent trouble sleeping (for example, most nights for several weeks, or affecting daytime function) is worth raising with a doctor. CBT-I is the standard professional route, but there's no source in this brief, so only say "talk to a doctor or sleep specialist."
- **Correlation, not causation.** Hjetland 2025 is cross-sectional; people with insomnia may use screens more, not only the other way round.
- **Breathing note:** Slow exhale-focused breathing is low-risk, but stop if you feel dizzy or lightheaded. Avoid breath holds or fast breathing at bedtime if you're pregnant, have heart or lung conditions, or have a history of fainting or panic. Keep it gentle and unforced.
- **If the wired feeling is anxiety or distress** that keeps coming back, point to a professional. If someone may be in crisis, point to local emergency services or 988 in the US.
- **Light sensitivity varies a lot** (Phillips 2019), so avoid "blue light doesn't matter." Say it's probably a smaller factor for most adults at typical brightness, and that some people are much more sensitive.
- **Don't recommend blue-light glasses**; no source here supports them.
- **Tone:** no guilt about minutes and no "ban your phone." Since the panel reached no consensus on adults, frame tips as options, not rules.
